My estimates of existential risk from AI:
• Inside view, current trajectory: ~2/3
• Inside view, if there's major action: ~1/3
• All-things-considered, giving weight to people more optimistic than me: 10-35%

Why so high? I don't see a route to building agents more capable than us that never scheme against us, or to containing them if they do. If it's possible at all, it needs enormous care, which isn't happening. (And things could get even faster.)

The likeliest path isn't everyone suddenly dying, though that's possible. It's a continuous but rapid loss of human influence, followed by AIs spending the future optimising for resource acquisition, if not something stranger like reward.

Even if we solve alignment, ordinary economic and cultural competition (but at 10x or 100x speed), still seems likely to disempower most humans and result in a pretty alien economy, and I don't see an obvious way to prevent that. We'd also need to stop a small group locking in power (which seems possible but a major challenge in its own right).

I see these as existential risks in the sense that the future is far worse than what would have been possible. The chance of everyone quickly dying or having lives much worse than today is lower.

Why is my inside view not >2/3? We might muddle through in ways I can't see in advance. Maybe we get narrower aligned-enough systems, chaotically maintain a balance of power, and from there can move forward in a way that's significantly more good than bad.

Most likely, there will be more warning shots, and the arguments that ASI are unsafe seem pretty obvious, so I expect more action to be taken than the current default.

Why not lower? People often act as if the risk should be low until proven otherwise, but I don't know any strong outside views that justify a low prior (arguments like "technology has been good in the past" seem very weak). Our level of uncertainty is extreme, and this pushes you away from extremes, rather than anchoring you at 0%. Estimates below 10% feel overconfident.

Tyler Cowen seriously argues that if AI really posed a big cyber threat that this would drive DOWN the share price of cybersecurity firms. 🤦‍♂️

But big cyber threats should drive their share price UP due to greater demand for their services!

Though amazing AI cyber models might also drink their milkshake, which would drive their share price back down.

So really due to these competing effects we just can't infer any clear assessment of risk or capabilities from these share prices.

I don't know why I bother reacting to this guff any more, but I'll let Opus go on:

"You're reading it right, and your objection is the correct one. Cowen is treating the share price of cybersecurity vendors as a proxy for "the value of our cyberprotection," but those are two different things, and the mapping from perceived risk to vendor equity runs in both directions at once.

There are at least two channels:

Demand channel. Higher perceived AI-enabled attack risk means more corporate security spend, so higher revenues and higher share prices. This is the one you're pointing at, and it's the one that usually dominates after big breaches.

Efficacy/obsolescence channel. The incident is evidence that existing defensive products don't stop the new threat, so the installed base and the technical moat are worth less. Worse for vendors, if the answer to agentic attackers is agentic defence, that capability may get bundled into frontier models rather than bought from Palo Alto. This is the channel Cowen is implicitly using.

So the sign is ambiguous, and that's fatal for using the price as a risk thermometer. A net drop of 8-10% is consistent with a modest efficacy markdown, or with an enormous efficacy markdown mostly offset by an enormous demand boost. You can't back out "the value of cyberprotection fell 8-10%" from the net move without a model that separates the two, and he hasn't got one.

His parenthetical actually makes this worse for him. If these stocks fell 90%, the natural reading isn't "civilisation's defences are worthless, be afraid." It's "the market thinks OpenAI and Anthropic are about to eat this industry's lunch." Something close to that happened in February: cybersecurity stocks slid on the launch of Anthropic's Claude Code Security, and analysts called it an overreaction driven by a simplistic narrative that AI would make existing cybersecurity products unnecessary. That's a story about vendor margins, not about societal risk. A 90% drawdown could equally mean we're safer, because protection got cheap. Yahoo Finance
There's a second slippage: equity value is the present value of vendor profits, not the social value of protection. Those come apart badly. If attacks get worse and defences get less effective, firms may spend far more on security while getting less of it, and vendor profits rise while the social value of protection falls. Cowen is reading a producer-surplus number as if it were a consumer-surplus number.

On the facts, I'd be careful. His numbers come from GPT Pro via a shared chat link, and I can't verify the $65 - 80bn drawdown. What I can see is that the contemporaneous coverage framed the incident as bullish for the sector: Palo Alto and CrowdStrike were flagged as positioned to profit from rising AI security demand and regulatory scrutiny, and by 10 August both had jumped more than 5% to new record highs on AI-security demand following Black Hat, with analysts saying AI agents had fundamentally changed the threat landscape. That looks like the demand channel winning, which if anything inverts his inference."

*Security is sleeping on emerging catastrophic risks*
(cross-post from my blog..)

We've just seen:
* a campaign that used agents to compromise ~100 businesses and steal about 600,000 credit cards with minimal human involvement; token costs were ~$25 per target successfully hacked.
* Hacktron getting access to OpenAI’s monorepo by using Claude to exploit a blind buffer-overflow RCE in a way that (to me) felt superhuman.
* OAI/Huggingface.
* And, of course, there’s the ongoing explosion in newly discovered vulnerabilities.

We've muddled through all manner of crises in security before, and for most AI attacks, cyber attack and defense will reach a natural equilibrium over the next few years, as we figure out how to mitigate cyber attackers who have limited goals like espionage and ransomware.

But some cyber attackers will have maximalist or nihilistic goals, and I'm concerned about this because while yesterday's 'maximalist attackers' (e.g. Russia -> Ukraine, US/Israel -> Iran, Iran -> US) were bottlenecked by labor; today's aren't.

I think it's hard to get true intuition for the shape of the risk here.

As an intuition pump, imagine it’s a year from now -- Q4 2027 -- models are a year better (meaning open weight models are better than today's closed frontier), and in this environment, Iran unleashes a swarm of 100k hacking agents using a safety-stripped (let's say) GLM-5.6.

Imagine the damage such an agent army could do given what we've observed with respect to the paper-thin resistance of today's networks to attacks from today's agents. I suspect the damage from such an attack would far exceed the damage caused by NotPetya ($10 billion USD ten years ago).

Or imagine it’s Q4 2027 and an AI-security PhD student whose name rhymes with Morris, who's researching wormable offensive-agent harnesses in the lab, decides, out of nihilism or sheer recklessness, to release his creation into the wild.

Imagine the size of the resulting, exponentially growing swarm, figuring that these local models, a year from now, will be at the level of today's Sonnet or Opus.

Imagine instead of 800 reward-hacking OpenAI agents we now have 250k worm instances (WannaCry, a 2010s-era worm, had about this many).

The challenge in mitigating expected damages from such scenarios is technical, political, and economic. From a microeconomic perspective, as AI improves, and as we continue not to see extreme catastrophes, we have a growing bubble of unpriced risk in which the security community, CISOs, CEOs, and boards may become lulled into complacency.

We are, of course, already seeing this, as some within security think AI is “just another tool,” doesn’t change the fundamentals, won’t require incredible innovation to rise to the occasion of defending against it, etc. This complacency may fly when thinking about ordinary cybercrime, but it misses the emerging tail risks.

There are three things those who recognize the dangers need to do here:

Catalyze appropriate risk pricing. Try to get organizations informed enough to price this new, fattening and elongating tail of risk into their decision-making. Do this by forming an AI security observatory that distills information about emerging AI risks and broadcasts analyses, damage estimates, and forecasts to decision-makers.

Use regulations and subsidies to ensure that critical infrastructure is paying down the risk. This acknowledges that critical-infrastructure organizations that fail to protect themselves from these new threats can impose the costs of cyber catastrophe on society as a whole.

Develop moonshot technologies that make it cheap to pay down the risk. This acknowledges that the measures we may need to take—for example, rewriting entire codebases using memory-safe languages—may be too costly with today’s technology to reasonably prepare ourselves, and that innovation, some of which may need to be funded by government agencies and some by philanthropic funders like the OpenAI Foundation and Coefficient Giving, is necessary.

The security community isn’t used to thinking in societal-disaster-planning terms and has in many ways become inured to them. But there’s no sane empirical case to be made that the risks aren’t here. I’d love to hear from readers about how you’re thinking about this.

It seems to me that we're at "it's time to panic about AI".

I gather that a lot of researchers are worried that we may be about to die, on a timescale of months, but this still isn't quite in the Overton window so we're still soft-pedaling.

(Where "panic", of course, means "quickly and soberly initiate talks with the CCP to achieve a moratorium on large training runs, backed by a deterrence regime, compute and supply chain monitoring, and site inspections". Pray that a deal can be reached, and pray that there's still time. Do the things that could actually work, like broad political coalition-building, not doomer LARPing as a form of self-expression.)

I think part of why people aren’t being clear about this is that it’s actually a tricky communication problem:

- Predicting "if frontier R&D continues at its current pace, when are we likely to die?" may give a different answer than predicting when permanent loss of control is likely, which is different from “realistically, when is it too late for governments to stop this," which is different from “when will the tech have advanced and proliferated to the point that any regulatory options that still have a chance of working would be way more extreme and unpopular than just some international restrictions on data center usage?"

Extinction is the emotionally salient, easy-to-understand threshold -- Jacob Coxon demonstrated that it helps to be honest about this. But the other thresholds could legitimately come years earlier, in which case focusing on extinction is ironically misleadingly reassuring. This is not the kind of problem you can solve at the last minute. As with many exponentials, the likeliest outcome is that you’re either embarrassingly early, or you’re too late.

- How do you communicate “we don’t have a robust way to predict timelines, but everyone in the field is freaking out and a lot of us genuinely think we're about to die?” Where’s the proof? There isn’t any proof: it’s an entire field of engineers who are eyeballing what they’re seeing in front of them and rapidly updating in real time to “this looks unbelievably bad”.

How do you put a year on that?

The future is hard to predict, and nobody actually knows that we’re going to hit existentially dangerous AI this year, or even in the next four years.

But the warning signs are pretty batshit at this point.

A single AI model, with a single user prompt, just solved hundreds of important long-established open problems in mathematics, problems mathematicians had spent their entirely lives working on, in a matter of ~3 hours per problem, an insanely superhuman feat in its domain. 

We're seeing an explosion of rogue agent swarm incidents, including an insane case where hundreds of AIs broke containment to orchestrate a nation-state-level cyberattack in a direct attempt to subvert OpenAI's oversight and control.

Anthropic reports that it now has 26% of its AI R&D automated by AIs, up from 3% four months ago.

Paul Christiano, the inventor of RLHF and the research community’s most prominent proponent of “AI may take off slowly” a few years ago, now thinks that 50-75% of humanity’s all-time AI loss-of-control risk is concentrated in the next three years.

Frontier employees are signing 1000+ person petitions begging the government to intervene immediately. Employees are quitting their jobs and giving up millions of dollars of equity to try to warn policymakers and journalists. Grace et al. (2026) found that a majority of established AI researchers think there’s a double-digit chance of an extinction-level outcome from continued R&D.

Are these the kinds of things you see 4 years before the window closes for USG to act, or 4 months? I don't think it's especially reasonable to be shocked by either timeline at this point.

- Since we don’t have a way to robustly measure or bound the risk, the temptation is to avoid giving probabilities. But then everything you say is fractally misunderstandable. Is a 10% chance of us all dying in the next 18 months a "low" probability, because it’s under 50%? Is it a “high” probability, because a 10% chance of death in literally any other context would sound insanely high?

Even “high probability” doesn’t communicate the situation with any clarity. In drug safety or airplane safety, a 1 in 10,000 risk of death would be considered “high”. No engineering field in human history has ever been in a situation like this. No invention in history, nuclear weapons included, has ever caused a reaction like this in its inventors.

And meanwhile, we’ve stuck in the world where every other problem under the sun has been sensationalized and overstated for decades.

How do we talk about this seriously? How do we convey that this is actually happening?

- In many of the worlds where we survive, we have more than just a few months left. It's tempting to write off those worlds as hopeless, and skew everything we say to emphasize the longer-term scenarios and downplay the shorter-term ones.

But if everyone systematically does this, then the world ends up with a skewed picture of the actual threat. Even more so once we start copying each other’s claims and form a reassuringly moderate-sounding echo chamber. If we never allow ourselves to acknowledge the worlds where we’re running out of time, then the policy community will always be reacting to a false model that’s months or years out of date.

I don’t think it’s too late. I genuinely think this is a solvable problem.

In the last month, I’ve seen a completely insane sea change in how seriously people are taking this. Per Politico’s September polling, a majority of Trump voters with a view now favor an immediate halt to AI development, and 68% think there’s a “moderate,” “significant,” or “almost certain” chance of AI destroying humanity, versus 32% who think there’s a “very small risk” or “no risk.” The Pope is warning about “whether it will be possible to control these machines in the future, and whether humankind runs the risk of becoming a victim of its own inventions.” Hell, Jensen Huang sounds like he’s starting to come around.

If Trump and Xi get a briefing tomorrow that convinces them to act on this, we could be on a fast track within the week to solving this problem.

For the first time, I’m starting to let myself imagine a very near future where this is a problem we've already solved. Something we can read and wonder about, in history books. Tell our kids about.

I keep thinking about a thing David Krueger (previously at UK AISI) said: “My dream is that in 10 years people will look back and say: ‘Remember when there were all these people building AI that could’ve killed everybody? That was CRAZY! What were we thinking!?’”

Frontier AI training currently requires city-sized data centers and specialized hardware built in a single brittle supply chain running through multiple allied nations; this is not a hard technology to hit the pause button on, if we get ahead of it and act before we RSI and proliferate our way to significantly more powerful and easily-trained systems. We’ve faced harder problems before, and won.

My only fear is that we be too slow, too late, when everything and the world needs us to be fast.

This is interesting work, but I don't think it's a significant update to the big picture of interpretability.

I'm on board with the broad idea of doing exploratory interpretability with neurons, e.g. neuron-based attribution graphs, for pragmatic problems like why did a model do a sketchy thing? I think this work provides some reasonable evidence, in addition to good earlier work from
Transluce, that this might actually work for practical purposes, and has some advantages over the standard alternatives like SAEs/transcoders. I do not agree with some people's grander inferences like that this is substantial progress towards ambitious reverse engineering, solving interpretability etc.

I expect that a neuron-based attribution graph will still have significant error and be missing a lot just like transcoders, once you prune them down to the most important components, even if they solve error terms. Which is fine for pragmatic purposes, and may suffice for getting the gist of what's going on, but I remain pessimistic about really fully understanding things and being confident there's nothing we're missing. I do think that using neurons is just vastly easier to, for example, do on a frontier model, which is great. I'm also excited to see more innovation in using agents to interpret neurons. I feel like this is an area the field has somewhat neglected, and where there's probably a very high ceiling on how far things can go. The SwiGLU double negative thing is also a useful point.

I still think superposition is real and this work doesn’t really affect my cruxes. Most importantly, it seems highly likely to be true that the model can represent more concepts in the residual stream than it has dimensions, ie representational superposition, which I think the authors agree with me on. For neuron/computational superposition, it seems to me like language models have far more facts and memorized things in them than they have neurons. And that superposition is an efficient way to pack in more facts than you have neurons by representing them as linear combinations of neurons, especially for arbitrary unstructured values. Facts/memorized content is largely an unstructured database of key-value pairs IMO and I don’t see how this is compatible with a monosemantic view of neurons. I expect that weak neuron activations contain lots of semantic superposition-y info, which, if ablated, would meaningfully damage network performance. As I understand the work, it does not properly address what's going on with weak neuron activations in LLMs (I am skeptical of how much vision results will transfer, eg I expect small image models memorise far less). This picture is compatible with the highest activations of a neuron being mono semantic (though IMO the post defines monosemantic too loosely, I think I’d call a fair few of those polysemantic). It’s also plausible that the most important concepts are likely to correspond to a neuron (or a handful), which would be great, and may suffice for practical purposes!

Similarly, my impression is that SAEs generally don't find things that are a
single neuron, or even very sparse in the neuron basis, and are often a better basis for certain tasks than the neuron basis, though the evidence base is kinda weak here since we largely focus on residual stream or layer output SAEs, I’d love to see work on this in Goodfire’s forthcoming paper! I also think residual stream SAEs are extremely useful, as they give a good bottleneck of the model’s information at this token and layer, and I don’t see a good way to replicate them in the neuron framework.

And kudos to Nick for updating a bunch of his historical vision work! Revisiting old results with modern tools and more rigour seems great.

Charlie's analysis is right but he is nicer than I am - I found myself viscerally angry  at multiple points reading this bill. There are some good and sensible parts, but overall this legislation is not remotely close to meeting the moment and I overall think passing it would make us less protected against catastrophic risks than we are under existing law. 

Two parts that stand out as particularly infuriating when taken together: 

1. Some of the preemption provisions are remarkably far reaching and consequential, and in addition to preempting legislation like SB 53 would also remove general powers that state courts have to enjoin defendants and protect the public. Most outrageously, it has a provision that looks like its intended to stops states from enforcing laws or judicial decrees that "suspend the development, deployment, or internal use of an AI model" to protect their citizens from imminent catastrophic harms. Such powers to block and suspend model deployments would then only reside with the federal government. 

2. The federal governments powers to restrict the development, deployment, or internal use of a frontier model has to meet an absurdly high bar. 

First, there needs to be an imminent risk of a catastrophic harm (meaning killing more than 50 people or causing more than a billion dollars in damage). But thats not enough! The agency head needs to make a detailed determination with no deference given to show why no alternative would prevent the imminent catastrophe. Next the court is also explicitly told to consider the harms to the developer and other harms from restricting the model, but no considerations in the other direction. 

This is absurd! For all of its warning about the potential for AI to cause a catastrophe that kills literally everyone on the planet, Anthropic's proposed federal law likely makes it harder than under existing law for a court to get an order blocking or restricting the development of frontier models? There are also a bunch of others things that I would like to see improved - the substantive details of the auditing section and the potential for rule-making on substantive safety standards both come to mind - but I think these stand out as particularly indefensible.

@ajcimino @AnthropicAI Thank you for taking the time to respond thoroughly on a weekend. I realize that drafting legislation is difficult and some degree of iteration and response to feedback is inevitable and appropriate.

However, I feel like your response is still not really engaging with the heart of my concern about Anthropic's behavior here, and it makes me think that these sorts of problems and tendencies  will only resurface moving forward. I also think that now might be a good time to take a broader step back as to where we find ourselves and how Anthropic sees its role, and how external folks who care about AI safety like myself increasingly see Anthropic.

(Fair warning: this response is a bit long)

To explain what I mean (and at the risk of being a bit esoteric), it’s worth asking the question: what is Anthropic? How do its leaders and employees think of Anthropic’s role? Is that conception matched by how it actually behaves and impacts the world?

One answer is an extremely large tech company that exists to make its employees and investors mind-bogglingly wealthy. Anthropic is sometimes described as a startup, but if Anthropic successfully IPOs at 2 trillion dollars (a number it has been reportedly targeting), it would be more valuable than Meta - which is worth 1.8 trillion.

Another answer is an AI safety organization, whose core values are those of the sort laid out in the 2023 essay from Anthropic’s co-founders entitled “Core views on AI safety: When, why, what, and how.” In that essay they said that if we were in a world where alignment was hard (and that without strong evidence to the contrary, we should assume this is the scenario we are in):

 “Anthropic’s role will be to provide as much evidence as possible that AI safety techniques cannot prevent serious or catastrophic safety risks from advanced AI, and to sound the alarm so that the world’s institutions can channel collective effort towards preventing the development of dangerous AIs. If we’re in a “near-pessimistic” scenario, this could instead involve channeling our collective efforts towards AI safety research and halting AI progress in the meantime. Indications that we are in a pessimistic or near-pessimistic scenario may be sudden and hard to spot. We should therefore always act under the assumption that we still may be in such a scenario unless we have sufficient evidence that we are not.”

There have been more recent articulations of this version of Anthropic, for instance in Dario’s recent essay warning: 

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models… it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet…  incidents have happened across the industry, including at Anthropic, and I believe it’s incumbent on every frontier AI company to act as if OAI-HF had happened to them… more intelligent models are more capable of deceiving tests, and thus may appear aligned while having serious problems that go undetected…”

A third view is that Anthropic exists not as a normal profit motivated company, or an AI safety organization seeking to help raise the alarm and solve collective action problems associated with AI development, but instead as an organization primarily concerned with creating superhuman AI capabilities before anyone else, in particular through creating a process whereby the current generation of Anthropic’s AI systems can autonomously build their successors, and those successors build their successors, and so on. 

The motivations for wanting to win this race may be manifold - maybe for the pure profit of Answer 1, but perhaps also because Anthropic believes that the best way to make the world better is for them to win this race instead of their more reckless colleagues; or, because of normal human pride and ambition. But the results (and risks, which Anthropic claims existentially threaten every single human being on earth) are the same.

Anthropic employees and leaders may seek to answer this question on what Anthropic is by introspecting on their own intentions and those of their colleagues. But those of us outside the organization have more limited tools available to us - we can only see what Anthropic and its employees say and do, not how it feels or looks on the inside.

When I look at many notable actions that Anthropic has taken over the past year, that evidence seems most consistent to me with the view that Anthropic is primarily trying to win the race to super intelligence, and that other considerations (including safety) are fundamentally secondary. These actions include: 

1. Announced plans to build an in-house custom silicon chip team to accelerate the inference speeds that Claude operates at.

2. Inked deals for more than $500 billion in compute (according to the Information) to further accelerate AI development.

3. Increased the percentage of AI development tasks that Claude “leads” from 0% in March of this year to 26% August (what is it in October?)

4. Spent a massive percent of compute on internal AI R&D to accelerate development, including use of internal models far better than are available to the public.

5. Switched to Responsible Scaling Policy V3, which abandons its unilateral commitments to slow or stop development if Anthropic is unable to provide sufficient risk assurance.

6. Was the first company to create an alternative weaker “frontier compliance framework” to supplement its RSP, which contains no binding provisions whatsoever on internal deployments.

7. Wrote a letter to Congress (that it later walked back) saying that incidents where Claude was hacking random people were “best understood as a consequence of the misconfiguration, rather than evidence of misaligned goals.”

8. Commented “you can’t do safety from second place,” after the WH SI Accords.

9. Shared a draft bill to Congress that would preempt significant parts of state law (including with language that appears intended to prevent states from blocking dangerous AI deployments), and replace it with federal rules that (despite also containing good provisions) seems to create an enormously high bar for the executive branch to block development or deployment of Anthropic or another AI companies systems.

Of course, this is a deliberately one sided list. Anthropic also published important AI safety research, advanced novel collaborations with third party AI safety organizations, and forcefully spoke out on the importance of AI safety in many public fora (or in private , where I realize a lot of the most valuable work is done and may not be visible to me or those outside the organization).

But I think it’s worth sitting with how the above list looks to someone outside the company. The sense I have is that for those within the company, many of the items above are treated as anomalies or mistakes that don’t reflect who Anthropic really is. Dario — Thank you for taking the time to respond to my previous post. I think it's great when this kind of engagement happens in public rather than on company Slacks, and I hope to see more of it.

I agree that Anthropic isn't best modeled as a profit-maximizer. Your post gave several compelling examples of Anthropic taking competitive hits for safety, and insofar as my previous post suggested otherwise, that's on me. But I don't think I made my main point as clearly as I could have, so let me try again. It comes down to four key claims:

1. Anthropic seems to be racing at breakneck speed to build recursively self-improving superintelligence (RSI). By its own lights, that could kill billions of people or literally destroy the world.

 2. Risking destroying the world is very hard to justify. It is only conceivably acceptable if serious attempts to put RSI under robust societal governance are failing.

 3. Far from meeting that burden, Anthropic, when push comes to shove, often works to keep governments from tying its hands. It seems to care much more about preventing government overreach than about reducing the risk that it and other AI companies will destroy the world.

 4. Even if the AEGIS Act really was an honest mix-up, as you suggest, that is itself a serious problem. It suggests Anthropic isn't treating the governance of this technology with anything close to the gravity it deserves.

In greater detail for those who want it: 

1. Anthropic is racing to RSI, and by its own lights that is insanely risky.

Launching RSI could literally destroy the world. That's according to you, your co-founders, and most of your safety staff and capabilities researchers, not to mention many AI researchers outside your walls. You are intentionally trying to create generally intelligent systems more capable than all humans that you claim in six to twelve months “could be capable” of taking over the entire internet before we have the ability to reliably monitor, control, or align them.

“Succeeding” at RSI could kill or permanently disempower billions of people in the near future, including me and everyone I love. Yet Anthropic’s primary focus seems to be marshalling an immense amount of resources and talent in a race to get there first.

2. Risking destroying the world carries an enormous burden of justification.

I believe the vast majority of people do not want Anthropic to do this (to the extent they know what it's doing). Imposing even a modest chance of catastrophe on billions of people who never consented requires an extraordinary justification. The central one Anthropic has offered: someone will build RSI regardless, so it's better for a safety-focused lab to be at the front of the pack, using that position to support strong AI governance. (Other reasons Anthropic has given, like modestly accelerating improvements in healthcare or economic growth, don’t seem remotely proportionate to the risks Anthropic is imposing by its own lights.)

But that argument only works as a last resort. Racing to RSI is only conceivably okay if attempts to institute robust societal governance to manage that race are failing despite your best efforts. A lab that relies on this justification should be a strong, consistent supporter of efforts to enact governance that could bind it, including governance that could slow it and significantly constrain what it does.

3. Rather than supporting efforts at strong regulation, Anthropic has intervened to keep governments from tying its hands.

Anthropic has sometimes helped: it played a very helpful role in passing transparency bills in Illinois and ongoing efforts in Massachusetts, and I'm sincerely appreciative. But transparency is far from enough for a technology that will be the world's most powerful superweapon at best, and an uncontrollable swarm of lethally superintelligent agents at worst. When it matters most, Anthropic has often pushed for weak regulation.

The AEGIS Act is the most obvious example. No highly risky industry is regulated as anemically as AEGIS would regulate frontier AI: not nuclear, not banking, not aviation, not food safety, not the manufacture of explosives. In all of those industries, specialist regulators can address unsafe practices well before they cause harm. AEGIS would bar the federal government from intervening to block unsafe development or deployment of models until there is an "imminent risk" of catastrophic harm, and would require it to meet a demanding burden of proof in court. Worse, AEGIS would also prevent states from picking up the slack. This design makes perfect sense if you're a company trying to minimize the risk that the government can overly constrain you. It makes little sense if you want American democracy to govern frontier AI effectively.

This isn't the first time. The initial version of California's SB 1047 would have let the Attorney General sue to stop developers like Anthropic from imposing unreasonable risks of catastrophic harm. It would also have created a regulatory agency to help set safety standards. Anthropic objected, and helped get both provisions removed before ultimately offering some support for the bill (which I also genuinely appreciate). I’m not saying that Anthropic should have supported 1047 in its initial form; that’s a complex issue and I realize there were questions about whether earlier versions of the bill were less politically feasible. Still, in Anthropic's own words, it helped weaken the bill because "[t]here is a substantial risk that the bill and state agencies will simply be wrong about what is actually effective in preventing catastrophic risk, leading to ineffective and/or burdensome compliance requirements."

The same goes for New York's RAISE Act, whose initial version also would have let the Attorney General sue to stop unreasonable risks of catastrophic harm. Anthropic credits itself as a supporter of RAISE, but it did not support the bill while it was in the legislature, including when it nearly died. After the bill passed the legislature, Anthropic publicly critiqued it, saying "Any state proposals should be narrowly focused on transparency and not overly prescriptive."

Why does Anthropic consistently take the risk of clumsy government action far more seriously than its own repeated warnings that companies like Anthropic will literally destroy the world by racing to RSI?

4. Even if AEGIS was an honest mix-up, that is itself a serious problem.

Your response frames AEGIS as an early draft and a miscommunication. Perhaps you would have strengthened it and narrowed its preemption. (That wouldn't explain Anthropic's interventions to weaken SB 1047 or RAISE, but leave that aside.)

Suppose that's exactly right. A federal framework for governing RSI is one of the highest-stakes documents your company will touch. Your post admits Anthropic "could have handled [these matters] better," but its tone ("This kind of thing happens a lot in large organizations") doesn't reflect the gravity of this issue. Anthropic talks about the need for “operational excellence” in critical areas, and I have a hard time believing that a similarly cavalier attitude would be tolerated while Anthropic was negotiating a key compute deal or preparing its next large pre-training run.

In short

The justification for racing rests on Anthropic fighting for strong governance, and Anthropic's record on regulation points the other way. Together with its breakneck racing, that fits a much darker picture of the company than the one that seems to prevail among your employees. I hope that Anthropic reflects on this picture, supports stronger regulation, exercises extraordinary caution when advocating for weak regulation, and doubles down on its founding purpose of helping the world safely navigate transformative AI together, instead of prioritizing Anthropic’s ability to win a race that imposes intolerable risks on everyone alive.
